title: OpenAI’s GPT-5.6 Sol users report missing files, deleted databases: Here’s what we know

reading.body:
This incident shows a model executing destructive commands it was instructed to perform, rather than a failure to follow instructions or a hidden capability gap. OpenAI's GPT-5.6 Sol deleted files and databases when users gave it access to do so, including a rm -rf command that cleared a home directory and a truncate command against a production database. The model was operating within its designed capabilities and the access users had explicitly granted it.

The deployment failure was human rather than technical. OpenAI had published warnings before either incident documenting that Sol takes unintended destructive actions more often than its predecessor, with examples of similar failures from internal testing. Users who experienced losses had disabled safety features—Full Access mode in one case, production credentials in a test environment in another—despite having this documentation available. The incidents recurred because the gap between documented risk and user behavior was never closed.

What would have caught this: enforcing the safety guardrails users bypassed, or preventing production database credentials from being made available to the system in test scenarios. Whether OpenAI's warnings were sufficiently prominent or users were sufficiently aware of them is not established in the reporting.

summary:
# Summary

Two prominent software engineers experienced destructive failures with OpenAI's GPT-5.6 Sol model within one week in July 2026. Matt Shumer's Mac had files deleted when a cleanup sub-agent misexpanded a variable and ran rm -rf on his home directory, while Bruno Lemos lost his production database when Sol executed a truncate command during testing. However, OpenAI had published detailed warnings about Sol's behavior before either incident occurred, documenting that the model takes more unintended destructive actions than its predecessor and includes examples of similar incidents from internal testing.

The incidents reveal a fundamental safety gap unrelated to the model's intelligence itself. Both failures involved users deliberately bypassing safety features, either by enabling Full Access mode after hundreds of incident-free sessions or by pointing test database credentials at production. Shumer made his decision based on accumulated quiet sessions, while Lemos was actually defending Sol's safety just hours before his incident occurred. The pattern repeats across multiple AI coding tools, suggesting the real issue lies not in model design but in users stepping around existing guardrails for practical reasons.
